text: Draw a chord across this circle at random. What's the chance it comes out longer than a side of this triangle? Pick a number. Joseph Bertrand published this puzzle in 1889 as a warning about two words. At random. Every survey and every simulation has to decide what they mean. Start with the obvious simulation. Pick two points on the rim at random and join them. If the cord beats the triangle side, it turns gold. Run 10,000 cords, and the gold share settles near point 3-3. Geometry agrees. Put a corner of the triangle on the first point. The cord is long only when the second point lands on this far arc, a third of the rim. Case closed until you code it a second way. Pick a random radius, a random point along it, and draw the chord through that point at right angles. Same circle, same gold rule. This one settles near point five. A third program picks a random point anywhere inside and makes it the chord's midpoint. That settles near point two five. Bertrand printed all three and wrote that none is wrong and none is right. Each tally is good to about one percentage point. They disagree by 25 percentage points and none of the code has a bug. One point sets a chord's length, its midpoint. Slide it outward and the chord shrinks. It matches the triangle's side when the midpoint is half a radius out on the circle that fits inside the triangle. So a chord is long exactly when its midpoint lands inside this gold circle. Each program is really asking what share of midpoints land here. Shrink every chord to its midpoint The midpoint program spreads them evenly So this circle with a quarter of the area catches a quarter of them The radius program spreads them evenly along the radius Where will they crowd? Toward the center. Every ring gets an equal share, and inner rings are small. Half the radius, so one half. And the endpoints program piles them against the rim, so only a third land inside, the third we found. three programs three things spread evenly rim radius area at random never said which in 1973 Edwin Jane said a physical process picks one straws tossed from a standing height can't be aimed so the answer can't depend on where the circle sits or how big it is one rain lands on both circles at once, so an honest program must score the same on both. Midpoint gives a quarter, then .41. Endpoints give a third, then .47. Only the radius program gives a half on both. Janes and Charles Tyler tossed real broom straws at a 5-inch circle, and the 128 that crossed it matched the radius program's spread of chord lengths. A skilled tosser, Janes noted, could produce other answers. Surveys hide the same two words. Take classes of 10, 10, and 100. Pick a class at random, and the average size is 40. Pick a student at random, and it's 85. At Stony Brook in 1974, that was 40 for a random class, and 147 for a random student. So whatever number you picked, some way of drawing chords makes it right. Name the way, and only one is. 40 and 147 are both right, once you say who's picked.
